stories.title: Tech leaders are celebrating Jensen Huang’s return
stories.summary: Let's say you're Jensen Huang. You (allegedly) cheated on your wife with an alleged Chinese spy, allegedly had an affair with not one, but two subordinates, and (allegedly!) stories.text:
Let’s say you’re Jensen Huang. You (allegedly) cheated on your wife with an alleged Chinese spy, allegedly had an affair with not one, but two subordinates, and (allegedly!) “terrorized” your employees, a series of indiscretions that led to your ouster from what was once the world’s most valuable company. (The stock price has recently taken a tumble, for obvious reasons.) And now you’re back, baby — and all your friends are so eager to congratulate you.

Huang is getting by with a little help from his friends.

Huang is getting by with a little help from his friends.

Elon Musk, for one, is thrilled.

And why wouldn’t he be? As a fellow leather jacket enthusiast who has a checkered history with women — including those who work for him — it’s clear that he and Huang have a lot in common beyond their positions as tech CEOs. Shivon Zilis, who has two children with Musk, also got in on the fun.

Gavin Baker, founder and chief investment officer of Atreides, is so impressed by Huang’s rise from the ashes that he’s going to buy a leather jacket of his own.

Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeny chimed in with an oblique reference to Huang’s outerwear.

Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke took what one could call a moral stance.

And then there’s billionaire investor Bill Ackman, a real wife guy if there ever was one, but one who, for better or worse, seems to understand that the market comes first.

Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire also pointed out the obvious market-bending powers of Huang’s reinstatement.

Of course, no one has been more effusive than the man who may have orchestrated it all. President Donald Trump posted his lengthy congratulations to Huang on Truth Social. “I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure,” Trump wrote. He commended Nvidia’s board for making the “correct and proper” decision in reinstating Huang — a decision that, the board admits, was made with input “from senior levels of the United States government,” who determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no security risk.” Isn’t that great news?

Trump expects Huang to make him proud. “I think you’re going to see some tremendous numbers out of this company,” Trump said on CNBC. “I talked to him last night. I said, ‘Jensen, just promise me one thing: You’re going to work hard.’ I spoke to him last night because I knew what was going on.” In the same appearance, Trump said “we need to protect our geniuses.”

Marc Andreessen didn’t officially comment on the reinstatement, but the a16z cofounder changed his X bio after the news broke. It now reads: “We have to protect our geniuses.”

Trump also seems to be relishing in Huang’s alleged affairs. In another Truth Social post, he superimposed Huang — red bra in hand — into the iconic photo of his reaction to being shot at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania.

For Canadian venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya, Trump’s intervention is just further proof of Huang’s innocence. Certainly an interesting take!

The market’s reaction may be the most jubilant of all. Per *Odd Lots*host Joe Weisenthal, NASDAQ-100 futures jumped so quickly that trading was halted. Congratulations to everyone who bought the dip, I guess.

*Update, November 23rd: This post has been updated with reactions from Shivon Zilis, Tobi Lütke, Shaun Maguire, Chamath Palihapitiya, and Marc Andreessen*.

stories.title: Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes
stories.summary: In separate but similar lawsuits filed on Monday, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones accused SpaceX of violating state consumer protection laws by ignoring industry-standard safeguards and falsely promoting the safety of its X social media platform and Grok AI features. The…
stories.text:
In separate but similar lawsuits filed on Monday, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones accused SpaceX of violating state consumer protection laws by ignoring industry-standard safeguards and falsely promoting the safety of its X social media platform and Grok AI features. The complaint filed in Virginia accuses Musk of willfully ignoring growing concerns around AI-generated sexualized deepfakes, and “instead saw a market opportunity for more profits,” describing the weak safeguards around Grok as “not a failure but a feature.”

State AGs called the weak safeguards built into Elon Musk’s AI image generator ‘not a failure but a feature.’

State AGs called the weak safeguards built into Elon Musk’s AI image generator ‘not a failure but a feature.’

“Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses. That was false. Instead, the tool permitted users to routinely create and circulate non-consensual intimate imagery and sexualized images, and child sexual abuse material (CSAM), causing harm to individuals and children,” Jones said in a press statement. “Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation.”

The complaints largely center around Grok Imagine, a tool that allows Grok and X users to generate images and videos. In August 2025, Grok maker xAI (which Musk has since merged with SpaceX) launched a “spicy” mode for Grok Imagine that spat out sexualized content including nude deepfakes of celebrities like Taylor Swift. In January 2026, Grok gained a feature that allowed X users to instantly edit any image without requiring consent from the original poster — resulting in X becoming flooded with nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes of adults and minors.

xAI made several changes to restrict access to Grok image editing, moving some capabilities behind a paywall and blocking certain requests for sexual poses, swimwear, or explicit scenarios. Our testing at *the Verge*following these restriction updates found they did little to prevent the bot from creating sexualized deepfakes, however.

Both of the Oregon and Virginia lawsuits are seeking financial damages.

The X Safety team said in a statement released after the lawsuits were announced that it takes appropriate measures to address users who generate sexual content involving minors:

“The people who tried to use Grok Imagine to generate this material did so by deliberately violating our Terms of Service and working aggressively to circumvent our safeguards. When some of these bad actors found ways to misuse Grok Imagine earlier this year, we acted promptly to tighten its protections, which are designed to refuse any request to generate explicit images of minors or real people. To stay ahead of this disgusting and indefensible conduct, we keep testing and adjusting those protections as these abusers change tactics. We also implement sophisticated classifiers that screen every prompt before an image is generated and check every output after.”

stories.title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix, and approve code changes
stories.summary: As AI-generated code piles up, Anthropic's new developer tools aim to eliminate another bottleneck by letting agents handle routine approvals.
stories.text:
Anthropic is moving from having Claude write code to helping developers decide when that code is ready to ship. On Monday, the newly public AI company announced the launch of Claude Ship, a suite of AI agents for automating code reviews, fixes, and approvals of routine code changes.

The latter is the more interesting part of this new set of tools, as AI coding tools already offered code review features before now. What’s notable about Claude Ship is not just that it can review proposed code changes and identify and address problems, but that it also includes an agent that can approve code changes automatically based on policies set by a development team.

The launch arrives at a time when AI coding agents have become increasingly capable of generating substantial amounts of code, leading to bottlenecks in reviewing and approving the code changes before they go live. With Claude Ship, the idea is to automate even more of the work involved in the development process, essentially by delegating approval authority to an AI agent itself.

“Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” a company blog post explains. “On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.”

Claude Ship is launching in beta, allowing early adopters to use it to review pull requests (PRs), and then decide what’s ready to merge.

The new offering consists of Code Review, which is already generally available, and two new agents now in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. PR Steward focuses on addressing issues such as failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and feedback from Code Review. It also comments after every push on what it changed and how to roll it back, if needed.

Claude Approvals then applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository. This approval process can incorporate various signals, including Code Review findings or the company’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language.

Because the offering is still in beta, Anthropic suggests running the approval functionality in observe-only mode first. Teams can also choose to start with just one repository and set monthly spending limits to have more control over the process.

Anthropic says teams will also still remain in control of where Claude Ship runs, which review settings to use (e.g., Quick, Standard, or Deep), and which changes should be escalated to a human for a decision.

Claude Ship is rolling out to Claude Team and Enterprise plans for repositories on GitHub. Code Review is generally available, while PR Steward and Claude Approvals are in beta.

stories.title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
stories.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here. Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model…
stories.text:
*This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, **sign up here**.*

Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.

Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.

This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll, 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).

But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness *is*, Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer.

You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with *Wired*last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea.

“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.

The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain *does*is equivalent to reproducing what a brain *experiences*.

But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models' production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “terrible” and “bizarre.” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet.

Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?”

It has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.

Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin. Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines. If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place.

Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers. This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement.

But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right. AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield. The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers. Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether. If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process.

Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size. But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

stories.title: Supertake raises $20M to let AI agents turn your market predictions into stock portfolios
stories.summary: Think you know where the market is headed? A startup called Supertake lets you put money behind your ideas without having to pick the stocks yourself.
stories.text:
AI investing startup Supertake has an interesting premise: What if your “takes” on the market could make you money without you having to pick stocks yourself? The service lets people turn their ideas into real investment portfolios, using frontier AI models and trading agents.

Now, the company has raised $20 million in seed funding to grow its business. The round was led by venture firm Adjacent (Nico Wittenborn), with participation from Coinbase Ventures and Union Square Ventures (USV). Numerous angel investors also joined, including Nat Friedman, who’s currently head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs; Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch; renowned product manager Nikita Bier; investor Scott Belsky; and Nemil Dalal, a former Coinbase exec who is now a visiting partner at Y Combinator.

Michael Mignano originally incubated the startup at USV. He is the co-founder and former CEO of the podcasting platform Anchor, which Spotify acquired in 2019 for over $150 million. After leading Spotify’s podcasting business as “Head of Talk” for a few years, he joined the team at Lightspeed as a venture partner, betting on AI companies like Suno and Granola. He also co-founded Oboe, an AI education startup, and joined USV as a general partner in April.

“We really believed there was an opportunity to make investing more democratized…and give everyone and anyone the ability to invest in their own insights and beliefs and ideas,” Mignano said. While he will continue in his role as founder and executive chairman, he’s now brought in a team to run the company day to day.

The team includes co-founders Lincoln Murr (CEO) and John Peterson (CTO). Both joined from Coinbase, where, Mignano notes, they were the heads of AI product and engineering, leading launches like Coinbase advisor, Coinbase for agents, agentic wallets, and others.

The startup arrives as AI continues to make inroads into financial services, but allowing AI to take over people’s actual investments requires a new level of trust. Supertake is betting that people will ultimately be willing to take that leap, given recent improvements in frontier AI models.

Currently, Supertake works with Coinbase and Robinhood, and the company intends to expand to more brokerages over time. The idea is that you can explain, in broad, natural language, what you believe about how the world is going to change, and Supertake’s AI will iterate with you back and forth to turn that idea into a “take” that’s investable.

Under the hood, the startup is leveraging frontier AI technology and tools, combined with its own proprietary software that directs and limits what the AI can do.

Supertake’s users’ ideas are tracked on a leaderboard on the site, so others who agree can invest alongside them. For instance, there’s currently an idea on the leaderboard about looksmaxxing and longevity becoming more of a trend, where the portfolio includes certain pharma and cosmetic companies that could potentially benefit.

For now, these portfolios consist of stock picks, but the team wants to expand the service over time to handle other types of transactions, like shorts, derivatives, perpetuals, long exposure, or even prediction markets — the latter handled through partnerships with companies in that space.

Despite these “takes” seeming like bets on what could happen next in a given market, Murr stresses that this doesn’t make Supertake itself a prediction market.

“We think it’s a novel and very much improved way to create what was previously considered the robo-advisor experience,” he says. “When that came out, it had this amazing vision and direction of allowing people to have digital asset management. We think now is actually the time for that, with AI agents being so widely proliferated.”

“I don’t think this is necessarily a prediction market by any means. The idea of natural language translation into an underlying set of assets feels different in that regard,” he says.

Still, the startup could wade into short-term predictions if a user’s take involves something they believe could happen in the near future, like who might win an election.

“We’re primarily focused on the longer, medium-term holdings today. But that being said, we don’t want to preclude people from building out very hyper short-term strategies that might exist,” Murr adds.

To address people’s concerns over AI managing their money, Supertake’s team says it’s implementing certain guardrails and spend limits. For instance, the AI has no ability to deposit or withdraw funds on a user’s behalf without their explicit consent. There are also drift limits in place so the portfolio stays balanced, plus allow and deny lists (meaning which assets the AI may and may not trade), real-time monitoring for anomalous activity, tools to set trade size limits, and a restriction that keeps agents from seeing the user’s brokerage credentials.

“We view it as somewhat analogous to self-driving cars, actually, where there is a spectrum here of both trust and technological innovations that are happening,” says Murr. “Where a few years ago you may not feel comfortable getting in a car that has lane assist, but today you get in a Waymo, and it’s like nothing. And we think that there’s a very similar progression happening with the agentic finance space, and we’re far further along in the technological spectrum than people think.”

Access to Supertake is still behind a waitlist while in beta, but the founders said they’ve put their money where their mouths are. Murr and Peterson are letting it manage “tens of thousands” and “thousands” of dollars, respectively.

Mignano, meanwhile, says he has Supertake managing “hundreds of thousands” of dollars.

With the new funding, which follows a $2 million pre-seed round, Supertake aims to expand its team in areas like engineering, design, growth marketing, and others. Mignano and Murr are in New York, while Peterson is in the Austin area but commutes to New York at times. The team says it hopes to figure out a hybrid work model as it grows.

stories.title: Qualitative User-Research Methods: An Overview
stories.summary: Want to know why users struggle or what they need? Start by choosing the right method. Here are 4 of the most popular qualitative UX-research methods.
stories.text:
This article covers 4 of the most popular qualitative-research methods: usability testing, user interview, field studies (including contextual inquiry), and diary studies.

This article is intended as a companion to Quantitative User-Research Methodologies: An Overview. As in the quant overview, we estimate the cost and difficulty of each method. These estimates are rough and relative. Your costs will depend on your tools, your participants, and how you adapt the method to your needs.

## Qualitative vs Quantitative Research

Qualitative and quantitative research answer different kinds of questions:

**Qualitative research**helps you understand people’s behaviors, experiences, needs, and problems. It answers*why*and*how*questions. Its findings are observations and themes, usually based on a small number of participants.**Quantitative research**measures. It reveals patterns and tells you how common a behavior or phenomenon is:*how many*,*how much*, and*how often*. Its findings are numbers, usually based on larger samples and analyzed with statistics.

The method alone doesn’t make a study qual or quant. Some methods, like usability testing, can be used for both. What makes the difference is your research question and how you set up the study. A qual usability test with a handful of participants looks for problems and their causes. A quant usability test with a larger sample (around 40 participants) measures metrics like success rate and time on task.

The two approaches complement each other: qual research tells you what’s happening and why, and quant research tells you how widespread it is.

## Why Qualitative Research

Most UX teams run far more qualitative (qual) studies than quantitative (quant) ones, and for good reason. Qual methods are flexible, relatively inexpensive, and useful at almost any stage of a project.

But because qual methods look simple (watch a few people use your site, talk to a few more), they’re also easy to get wrong. Pick the wrong method or run the right one carelessly, and you’ll end up with misleading findings and a false sense of confidence. Done well, qual methods allow you to:

**Discover**what’s wrong with a design and why.**Understand**your users’ needs, goals, pain points, and mental models before you design anything.**See**how people really behave in their own environments, including the workarounds, interruptions, and extra tools they rely on.**Build empathy**across your team. Watching a real person struggle with your product is often more persuasive than any report.

## Choosing a Method

This table summarizes the methods discussed above. Costs and difficulties are general comparative estimates; ultimately, the cost of a study will depend on its goals and specific setup.

To pick the right method, lead with your research question. What do you need to know?

If you want to find problems in a design and understand why they occur, you have an **evaluative question**. For example:

- Do people find and understand the shipping costs before they reach checkout?
- Why are users abandoning our signup form?
- Which parts of our new prototype confuse people?

For these questions, you’ll likely want to use **qualitative usability testing**. (Note, if you want to measure how well a design performs, such as its success rate or time on task, you need quantitative usability testing instead.)

If you’re trying to understand people’s needs, behaviors, and experiences, you have a **generative question**. For example:

- What are the biggest frustrations people have when planning a vacation?
- How do nurses use patient records during a shift?
- How do people decide which meal-delivery app to use, and does that change over time?

For these questions, you’ll probably want to use **user interviews, field studies, or diary studies**. To choose among them, ask yourself:

**Do you need to see what people do, or is hearing about it enough?**Interviews are efficient but rely on people’s memories. If accuracy about real behavior matters, observe.**Does the environment matter?**If tools, interruptions, or other people shape the experience, or if accuracy about real behavior matters, run a field study. (For complex or expert work, consider contextual inquiry.)

**Does the experience unfold over days or weeks?** If so, a diary study will capture it better than any single session.

## Qualitative Usability Testing

**Use:**Identifying problems in a design and understanding why they occur**Cost:**Low–Medium**Difficulty of Collection:**Medium**Difficulty of Analysis:**Low–Medium**Type of Method:**Behavioral (what people do)**Context of Use:**Task-based**Typical Sample Size:**About 5 participants per user group, per round of testing

In a usability test, a facilitator asks a participant to perform realistic tasks using a design, then observes what the participant does and listens to what they say. Participants are usually asked to think aloud — to narrate their thoughts as they work — so you can hear their expectations, confusion, and reasoning in the moment.

Qual and quant usability testing look alike on the surface, but they have different goals. Quant usability testing collects metrics like success rate and time on task. Qual usability testing prioritizes observations: Where did people get stuck? What did they expect to happen? Why did they choose the wrong link? Because the goal is insight, not measurement, the facilitator can ask followup questions and adjust the study as it goes.

You don’t need many participants. For a typical qual study with a single user group, testing with 5 users uncovers many of the common usability problems in a design. Testing with additional participants generally has diminishing returns, so rather than spending your budget on one big study, test with a few people, fix what you found, and test again.

Qual usability testing works at any stage, from paper prototypes to live products. You can run sessions in person, remotely with a facilitator, or remotely without one. Each format changes the cost and the amount of control you have over the session.

The biggest risk is accidentally influencing participants. Small wording problems in your tasks can prime people to look for a specific word or feature, and an untrained facilitator can change participants’ behavior by interrupting at the wrong time. Good facilitation takes practice.

For the skills you need to plan, facilitate, and analyze usability tests, see our course Usability Testing.

## User Interviews

**Use:**Learning about users’ experiences, needs, pain points, and motivations**Cost:**Low**Difficulty of Collection:**Medium**Difficulty of Analysis:**Medium**Type of Method:**Attitudinal (what people say)**Context of Use:**Not using product**Typical Sample Size:**Often 5–12 for a focused study; 20–30 or more for a broad one

In a user interview, the interviewer asks a participant questions about a topic, listens to their responses, and follows up to learn more. Interviews are especially useful in the discovery phase, when you’re trying to understand who your users are, what their lives are like, and what problems you could solve for them. The insights often feed into artifacts like personas and customer-journey maps.

User interviews are often confused with usability tests, but the two methods serve different purposes. A usability test evaluates a design by observing how people use it. An interview generates new knowledge about people’s experiences; participants usually don’t see or try a design at all.

A good interview is a research study, not a casual chat. Start with clear research goals, then write an interview guide with a few open-ended questions that get people talking. Ask about specific events rather than general habits. For example, *Tell me about the last time you booked a vacation*will produce richer, more accurate details than *How do you usually book vacations?*Then probe with followup questions like *Tell me more about that*or *Why was that important to you?*

How many people should you interview? It depends on how broad your research goals are and how varied your users are. Five interviews are sometimes too few for exploratory research. Start with a small sample (5 or 6), analyze as you go, and add participants until you stop learning new things.

Interviews have an important limitation: they collect *reported*behavior, not *observed*behavior. People forget details, leave out things they don’t realize are relevant, and sometimes present themselves in a flattering light. And the quality of the data depends heavily on the interviewer’s skill. A few leading questions can undermine an entire study. When you need to know what people actually do, pair interviews with an observational method.

For hands-on practice planning and conducting interviews, see our course User Interviews.

## Field Studies (Including Contextual Inquiry)

**Use:**Understanding users’ real environments, workflows, tools, and workarounds**Cost:**Low-High**Difficulty of Collection:**High**Difficulty of Analysis:**High**Type of Method:**Behavioral and attitudinal (mostly what people do)**Context of Use:**Natural use**Typical Sample Size:**Small; recruit until you reach saturation

A field study takes place in the user’s natural environment (their home, office, car, store, or hospital ward) rather than in a lab or conference room. Field studies and diary studies are both context methods: they show you how people behave in real life, not in a hypothetical scenario you’ve set up for them.

Context reveals things you wouldn’t know to ask about. When you watch people in their own environment, you see the sticky notes on their monitors, the spreadsheet they keep open next to your app, the coworker they turn to for help, and the constant interruptions that pull them away from their tasks. You also see the gap between what people say they do and what they actually do.

Field studies range from fully immersive to tightly focused. Common types include:

**Direct observation:**The researcher watches without intervening or asking questions.**Contextual inquiry:**The researcher combines observation with in-the-moment questions.**Customer-site visits:**The customer leads the researcher through their facility or system.**Ethnography:**The researcher immerses themselves in a group’s setting for an extended period.

Whichever type you choose, prioritize observation over questions. Once you’ve gone to the trouble of visiting someone in person, the most valuable data you can collect is what they do.

Field studies can be expensive to run if they require a lot of travel to reach your users. They can also be challenging to set up logistically because they may require permissions and scheduling around participants’ work. Finally, they can be challenging to analyze because of the amount of unstructured data they produce. But a simple field study doesn’t require a team of anthropologists. Everyone on a design team can and should go on customer visits from time to time.

### Contextual Inquiry

Contextual inquiry is one of the most useful field methods for UX teams. It combines in-depth observation with interviews to understand people’s work practices and the reasoning behind them, and it can sometimes be done remotely. The method is based on the relationship between a master craftsperson and an apprentice. The participant (the master) does their work as usual. The researcher (the apprentice) watches, then pauses to ask questions when something is unclear or to check an interpretation. Sessions usually follow 4 parts:

**Primer:**Build rapport, explain the session, and get a summary of the work.**Transition:**Explicitly shift from interviewing to observing, so the participant knows to work normally while you watch.**Contextual interview:**Alternate between watching and discussing what you’ve seen.**Wrapup:**Summarize your interpretations so the participant can correct or confirm them.

Contextual inquiry is powerful because, as people do a task, they can describe what they’re doing and why — details that they may struggle to recall later. In one redesign project, insurance specialists described a simple copy-and-paste process during interviews. Observing them at work revealed extra steps they hadn’t mentioned, such as checking a second application for missing information and repeatedly clicking *Save*even though the software saved automatically. Both insights shaped the new design.

Contextual inquiry is best suited for complex systems, in-depth processes, and expert users. It’s overkill for simple interfaces, like a newsletter-signup form.

A common pitfall: participants may slip into interview mode and start summarizing their work instead of doing it. A clear transition (and gentle reminders to work as usual) helps.

For more on field studies and other discovery methods, see our courses UX Research Methods: From Observation to Insight and Discovery.

## Diary Studies

**Use:**Understanding behaviors and experiences over time and in context**Cost:**Medium**Difficulty of Collection:**High**Difficulty of Analysis:**High**Type of Method:**Attitudinal and self-reported behavioral (what people say they do)**Context of Use:**Natural use**Typical Sample Size:**About 5–12 for small discovery projects; 12–30 for large ones

In a diary study, participants log their activities and experiences as they happen, over a period of days, weeks, or even a month or longer. For example, you might ask people to report every time they use a meal-delivery app over 3 weeks, or ask nurses to log every interaction they have with patient-health records.

Diary studies capture something no single-session method can: how behaviors and perceptions change over time. They’re a good fit for research questions about habits, long customer journeys, how people learn a system, and how they move between channels and devices.

Like field studies, diary studies are a context method. But because they’re run remotely and asynchronously, they’re usually cheaper than field studies and make it easier to include participants in many locations.

Unlike field studies, diary studies rely on self-reporting rather than observation. Because the participants report events close to when they occurred, a diary study somewhat reduces the recall problems associated with interviews. But it does not completely remove self-report biases.

Participants typically create entries in one of three ways:

**Event-based:**They log an entry whenever a relevant event occurs.**Interval-based:**They log an entry at regular intervals (for example, every evening).**Signal-based:**They log an entry whenever you prompt them (for example, by text message).

Diary studies require a lot of planning. You’ll need to choose a logging tool, write clear instructions and example entries, and decide on a reporting period long enough to capture the behavior you care about. Plan to monitor entries as they come in, so you can ask followup questions while the experience is still fresh. Many diary studies also start with a pre-study briefing and end with a followup interview to explore each participant’s entries in depth.

Because participants are committing to days or weeks of effort, expect some to drop out. Overrecruit, and offer higher incentives than you would for a single session.

The data is all self-reported, so diary studies share some of the limitations of interviews. And they generate a lot of qualitative data: set aside plenty of time to analyze it.

## Combine Methods

You rarely have to pick just one method. Some combinations work especially well:

- Start a usability test with a short interview to learn about the participant’s background (but avoid questions that draw attention to parts of the design you’re testing).
- Interview participants before or after you observe them in the field.
- Bookend a diary study with a kickoff briefing and a followup interview.
- Follow a qual study with a quant one to learn how common your findings are. (See Quantitative User-Research Methodologies for options.)

## Consider Time and Cost

After the research question, budget and time are usually the next biggest factors.

Qualitative usability testing and user interviews are the least expensive and quickest methods here. A simple usability study can take as little as 3 days of your time: one to plan, one to test, and one to analyze. Remote sessions can lower costs further by eliminating travel and lab rentals.

Diary studies cost more than single sessions because of the higher incentives, the time needed to monitor participants, and (sometimes) specialized software. Field studies can be the most expensive if they require a lot of travel. If you can’t afford to go into the field, a remote diary study can give you some of the same contextual insights.

The number of participants included in the study also contributes to the cost. Sample sizes work differently in qual research than in quant research. Instead of calculating how many participants you need for statistical significance, researchers using generative methods (interviews, field studies, and diary studies) aim for **saturation**.

Saturationis the point in a qualitative study where additional sessions no longer produce new insights that would change your themes.

Saturation can be achieved with just a few participants when research questions are fairly narrow (e.g., how nurses hand off patient records at a shift change). Broader goals or more varied users need more participants (e.g., how people use personal assistants).

Qualitative usability testing is a little different. Rather than running one large study until you stop finding new issues, we recommend **spreading your budget across several small rounds of testing**: test with a few users, fix the problems they uncovered, and test the revised design. The first few users in a round reveal most of the common problems, so each additional user mostly repeats what you’ve already seen. A new round, on the other hand, shows whether your fixes worked and uncovers problems that the earlier ones hid. That’s why we recommend 4–6 users per round.

### Next Steps

Once you’ve picked a method, learn about it before you start. We’ve included links throughout this article, as well as a *Resources*section at the end.

Be warned: **Qualitative doesn’t mean casual.** Qual findings are based on the researcher’s observations and interpretations. Unlike quant data, they don’t come with statistical protection against chance. That means rigor matters at every step:

- Write clear research goals before you plan your sessions.
- Recruit participants who represent your actual users.
- Avoid leading questions and other behaviors that bias participants.
- Analyze your data systematically (for example, with thematic analysis or affinity diagramming) rather than relying on the most memorable quotes.

It takes practice to do qual research well. But it’s the most direct way to learn what your users need and why your designs do (or don’t) work for them.

stories.title: Can AI Generate Good Designs from Raw User Data?
stories.summary: In our study, AI-generated designs were better when the AI received synthesized findings and recommendations instead of raw user comments alone.
stories.text:
AI can now analyze user data, provide design recommendations, and generate interfaces all in one go. So, is it still worth synthesizing research and developing recommendations first, or can teams hand AI the raw data and let it decide which user problems matter and how to solve them? The answer matters more and more as AI-generated prototypes become part of everyday design work.

To find out, we asked an AI model to generate interfaces from different types of research context. Across two design tasks, **it produced better designs from synthesized findings and recommendations** than from raw user comments.

## About the Study

We gave an AI model two design tasks: designing a one-page form for rebooking a canceled flight and designing a multistep checkout flow for an online store. In each task, the prompt and the design-system information remained the same, while the type of research context we provided to the model changed.

While the actual study design was more complicated, in this article we will focus on two types of context that the AI model received:

**Raw user comments**, which included approximately 100 comments for each design task**Synthesized findings and recommendations**based on the same raw user comments (A researcher analyzed the comments with an AI tool and made the final decisions on which findings to include and what to recommend).

Since AI tools are nondeterministic, we generated 8 designs per task and context condition. Then, a human grader and an LLM judge blindly scored each design against a predefined scorecard. The score of the design was the percentage of scorecard criteria it met (e.g., “every checkout step shows the items being bought”).

We used the human grader's scores in the results. The LLM judge scored every design independently as a check, and after calibration, the 2 graders agreed on about 96% of scoring decisions in both tasks.

Details on the study methodology are available in the accompanying sidebar.

## Synthesized Findings and Recommendations Led to Better Designs

Across both design tasks, **the AI-generated designs based on synthesized findings and recommendations met more scorecard criteria than designs based on raw user comments**. The average difference was 8.4 percentage points and was statistically significant (p < 0.001).

The improvement was larger for the flight-rebooking task (11.4 percentage points compared to 5.5 percentage points for the checkout flow), but both tasks benefited. The finding suggests that **design generation with AI can benefit from the work of synthesizing research data into findings and recommendations**.

The flight-rebooking task shows what this difference looked like in practice. A few raw comments complained about loyalty miles, yet none of the designs generated from raw comments included information on whether the cancellation would affect passengers’ miles. In contrast, every design generated from synthesized research included that information.

The online-checkout task showed a smaller gain for the synthesized research but the same pattern. Several user comments complained that items disappeared from the cart during checkout, yet fewer than half of the designs based on raw data kept the items and total visible on every checkout step. Nearly all the designs made from synthesized research did. The smaller gain may be due to the task prompt, which was the same in both conditions and already pointed to some of the issues raised in the comments: It described a first-time shopper with a discount code who needed a gift within 2 days. Because the prompt itself flagged concerns such as applying a discount and receiving the order on time, even the designs made from raw comments tended to address them, leaving less room for synthesized research to make a difference.

The 8.4-percentage-point advantage of synthesized findings and recommendations may underestimate their benefit in more complex situations. First, our data was likely cleaner than typical user feedback. Although cleanliness is hard to measure, more than half of the comments in each task supported a finding, whereas research on app-store reviews found that only about a third of reviews contained information useful to product teams. Second, the dataset was small, about 100 short comments per task. Third, both tasks (designing a form and a checkout flow) are common patterns that AI models have likely seen many times. **We expect the advantage of synthesized research to grow with larger, messier datasets and less familiar design problems**,** **and we plan to study this hypothesis in the future.

## Why Might Synthesized Research Improve AI-Generated Designs?

### Raw Data Contains Observations Only

Raw user data describes problems, such as what frustrated users and what they wished worked differently, but it rarely says what to build in response. For example, a comment such as "Items disappeared from my cart" names a problem but does not mention a solution. Even when users suggest a fix, the suggestion isn’t a reliable guide. Users are good at describing their problems, but they’re poor at predicting what they would actually use, and what they say doesn’t always match what they do.** **Raw data also tends to be messy. It can include comments unrelated to the design, and different user comments may contradict each other.

### Synthesized Findings and Recommendations Add a Layer of Interpretation

When working only with raw data, the AI needs to decide which data points matter and what changes to make. Those decisions are difficult because user feedback is only one input. In real life, designers weigh user feedback against business needs, technical constraints, product goals, and what the team has already tried. AI tools struggle with those tradeoffs without human guidance.

Through findings and recommendations, researchers apply their judgment to turn raw data into design decisions.** **They add a layer of interpretation that can help the AI generate the right design. Without them, you leave those decisions to the AI.

Findings and recommendations play different roles, though. Findings interpret the data, while recommendations turn that interpretation into design decisions. Because our analysis compared raw user comments with synthesized findings and recommendations, we don’t know at this point whether the improvements were caused by the findings or by the recommendations. We are working on determining the effect of each in a separate study.

## Implications for Product Teams

Research artifacts now have two audiences: your teammates and the AI tools used in the design process. Along with artifacts created for people, we also must create artifacts that guide AI tools.

### Don’t Assume Raw Research Data Is Sufficient Context

AI tools can process substantial amounts of user-research data, but that doesn't mean they will automatically identify the most important information and use it appropriately in a design. Consider what interpretation and guidance the AI tool needs rather than assuming access to the underlying data will be sufficient.

### UX-Context Design: Think About What UX Knowledge AI Needs

As AI becomes more involved in generating interfaces, we will increasingly need to figure out what guidance and knowledge to provide to these tools. The context that you give an AI tool shapes what it creates. UX-context design is the practice of selecting, organizing, and maintaining the UX knowledge that guides AI-generated design. This study offers evidence that the content of this context can affect design quality.

## Ongoing Research

This study raised several questions that we’re still exploring.

- Do synthesized research and recommendations improve design quality only on the specific issues addressed by the findings and recommendations, or in other respects too?
- Do the results hold for other types and larger volumes of raw data than short customer comments, such as interview transcripts, usability-test notes, or survey responses?
- Would other AI models produce the same results?
- How much of the benefit comes from the synthesis of the findings versus from including explicit design recommendations?
- Does the format of the file (e.g., Markdown, PNG, PDF) in which the context is provided make a difference?

We’ll keep studying how teams can give AI better UX context, so look out for future articles on these topics. To start applying these ideas now, see our Context Engineering: Shaping AI-Generated Designs course.

### Conclusion

As AI takes on more of the design work, steering what it produces matters more. Our findings suggest that not all context is equally useful. Providing AI with synthesized research findings and recommendations leads to better designs than providing it with raw user comments alone. At a time when AI is raising questions about the future of UX, this finding is important. Generating an interface is just one part of design. Understanding which user problems matter for your product and translating that understanding into design recommendations remain an essential contribution of UX professionals, whether the designs are created by humans or AI.

### References

Ning Chen, Jialiu Lin, Steven C. H. Hoi, Xiaokui Xiao, and Boshen Zhang. 2014. AR-miner: Mining informative reviews for developers from mobile app marketplace. In *Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE 2014)*, 767–778. https://doi.org/10.1145/2568225.2568263

stories.text:
AI is changing how we design and build, and it isn’t slowing down. On December 1, 2026, SmashingConf is hosting the AI 2027 Conference, a live online half day event to take stock of where AI stands today, what we can expect in 2027, and where teams are getting it right.

With AI maturing, it’s clear we need to learn how AI can elevate your workflow as a UX designer and Design System engineer. Most of us are still figuring it out and trying to work smarter in this new world, so we invited industry experts who have been doing this for a while. They show their experience and tell you **what works and what doesn’t**, so you don’t have to figure it all out yourself.

Every session is practical. Speakers show how they actually work: their tools, their setups, and the small things that are easy to miss. The event ends with moderated breakout rooms, where **you can bring your own workflow questions**. See you there?

## About AI 2027 Conf And Schedule

This conference is dedicated to designers and engineers (front-end, UI, UX) who want to understand how AI can improve the way their team works, without the hype. If you’re interested in AI-ready design systems, AI and Figma, harness engineering, agentic AI UX patterns, and AI workflows for design and engineering teams, this conference is right up your alley!

**Showing, not telling**: All sessions will be highly practical, focusing on how to integrate AI in your daily work and what to expect in 2027.

stories.title: 2.3 million end-of-life vehicles still plying in NCR: CAQM tells SC
stories.summary: More than 2.36 million end-of-life vehicles remain active in Delhi-NCR, while only 185,000 were scrapped or moved out between January and October 2026.
stories.text:
Utkarsh Anand is the National Legal Editor at Hindustan Times, where he leads the newspaper's coverage of the Supreme Court, constitutional law, the judiciary and the Union law ministry. He joined Hindustan Times in 2020 after stints at Press Trust of India (PTI), The Indian Express and CNN-News18, and has over two decades of experience reporting on law, governance and public policy. His work has focussed on some of India's most consequential constitutional and legal developments, including the Supreme Court's judgments on Article 370, marriage equality, decriminalisation of homosexuality, the Babri Masjid dispute, electoral reforms and judicial appointments. He specialises in making complex legal proceedings and judgments accessible to readers while examining their wider social and political impact. Beyond daily reportage, Utkarsh has led investigative projects and enterprise reporting that have shaped public debate and prompted institutional responses. His work has received several journalism awards, including the Ramnath Goenka Excellence in Journalism Award. As National Legal Editor, he has also played a key role in expanding Hindustan Times' legal journalism footprint, mentoring reporters and strengthening coverage across platforms. A Chevening South Asia Journalism Programme Fellow, Utkarsh regularly writes analyses on the judiciary and constitutional issues, and his reporting is widely followed by lawyers, judges, policymakers, academics and readers seeking clarity on India's evolving legal landscape.

## More than 2.36 million end-of-life vehicles remain active in Delhi-NCR, while only 185,000 were scrapped or moved out between January and October 2026.

More than 2.36 million end-of-life vehicles (ELVs) remain active across Delhi-NCR, exposing the scale of the challenge in tackling vehicular pollution, even as nearly 94% of the 17.1 million vehicles registered in the region are two-wheelers and cars, the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) has told the Supreme Court.

In its affidavit, the commission said that of the 2.54 million overaged vehicles reported across Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, and Rajasthan, only 185,000 had been scrapped or issued no-objection certificates to move out of the region between January and October 2026, describing the progress made by the states as “far from satisfactory.”

In a status report filed in the court’s ongoing suo motu proceedings on vehicular emissions, the commission said two-wheelers account for 65.2% of the total vehicle population in Delhi-NCR, while four-wheeler light motor vehicles make up another 28.9%.

The figures, based on data available on the VAHAN portal as on October 31, 2026, show the region has 11,205,160 two-wheelers and 4,959,087 light motor vehicles (LMVs) out of a total 17,176,234 registered vehicles. Three-wheelers account for 1.9%, buses 0.3%, and goods carriers 3.7%.

The commission, however, cautioned that the pollution potential of vehicles varies substantially according to their emission standards, with older vehicles emitting considerably higher quantities of pollutants than those conforming to Bharat Stage-VI, or BS-VI, norms.

Highlighting the problem posed by older vehicles, CAQM said BS-II emission standards came into force in April 2001, BS-III in April 2005 and BS-IV in April 2010.

The commission pointed out that BS-II standards came into force in April 2001, BS-III in April 2005, and BS-IV in April 2010. BS-VI standards were introduced in Delhi from April 2018 and the rest of NCR from April 2019. This means BS-III vehicles have been on the road for over 15 years, BS-II for over 20 years, and BS-I for over 24 years.

The report provided a comparison showing older vehicles can emit several times more pollutants. Diesel LMVs and light commercial vehicles complying with BS-IV emit nitrogen oxides at 3.13 times the BS-VI level and particulate matter at 5.55 times. For BS-III vehicles, the corresponding emissions are 6.25 times and 11.11 times higher. Diesel vehicles conforming to BS-II emit NOx at 8.75 times and particulate matter at 17.77 times BS-VI levels, while BS-I vehicles emit 12.13 times more NOx and 31.11 times more particulate matter.

CAQM said the fitness of a vehicle should not be viewed independently of its emission potential, as even a vehicle that is otherwise fit would continue to emit pollutants in accordance with the standards under which it was manufactured. “Since Delhi-NCR faces an extraordinary situation, especially during winter due to poor dispersal of pollutants, there is a need to restrict plying of polluting vehicles based on emission standards,” the commission submitted.

**Slow progress in scrapping**

Delhi has 852,396 active end-of-life vehicles, of which only 62,546 were scrapped and another 7,230 issued NOCs to move out during 2026 till October. Haryana has 988,368 active ELVs, with 16,135 scrapped or issued NOCs. Uttar Pradesh reported 589,979, of which 97,998 were scrapped or moved out, while Rajasthan had 112,936, with only 2,047 accounted for.

The commission said the progress made by all four jurisdictions in dealing with end-of-life vehicles had been “far from satisfactory”.

Among the measures already undertaken, CAQM said it had directed that only CNG or electric auto-rickshaws be registered across the NCR from January 1, 2023, with a phased elimination of diesel auto-rickshaws. It has also mandated a phased transition towards electric three-wheelers, with new registrations of only electric L5-category three-wheelers to be permitted in Delhi from January 1, 2027.

The commission has further directed that only CNG, electric or BS-VI diesel inter-city buses be allowed to enter Delhi from November 1, 2026, including buses operating under All India Tourist Permits and other service categories. Similarly, commercial goods vehicles other than BS-VI, CNG, LNG and electric vehicles have been barred from entering Delhi from November 1, 2026, subject to the applicable exemptions.

The report also highlighted the Delhi government’s Electric Vehicle Policy 2026, which provides for new registrations of only electric L5 three-wheelers from January 2027 and electric two-wheelers from April 1, 2028. It also envisages phased electrification targets for commercial fleet operators, logistics aggregators and private schools.

CAQM said the transition to electric mobility must be accompanied by adequate charging and battery-swapping infrastructure. As on October 31, Delhi had 683,251 electric vehicles and 14,913 charging stations or points. Uttar Pradesh had 347,587 electric vehicles and 565 charging points, Haryana 218,530 electric vehicles and 1,285 charging points, while Rajasthan had 44,987 electric vehicles and 22 charging points.

The commission has also recommended a series of long-term interventions, including a time-bound phase-out of polluting vehicles based on their emission potential, stronger pollution-under-control certification mechanisms and monitoring of on-road emissions through remote-sensing devices.

Other recommendations include expanding metro and regional rail networks, developing multi-modal transport hubs connecting metro and the Regional Rapid Transit System, improving last-mile connectivity and expanding electric bus services.

It has also called for a wider network of EV charging and battery-swapping facilities, incentives for scrapping older vehicles, and permission for retrofitting existing vehicles to electric mode subject to certification by the Automotive Research Association of India or the International Centre for Automotive Technology.

On the enforcement front, CAQM has proposed technology-driven surveillance through automatic number plate recognition cameras, radio frequency identification systems, remote-sensing techniques and artificial intelligence-based monitoring.

A significant part of the commission’s recommendations concerns decongesting Delhi’s border entry points, where prolonged stoppages of vehicles contribute to pollution. It has recommended installation of barrier-free Multi-Lane Free Flow systems integrated with RFID and ANPR technology at all toll collection points.

The commission has suggested that if the system is not fully operationalised within the prescribed timeline, toll collection at nine identified toll plazas during the peak winter months of November to January should be restricted to vehicles liable to pay the Environment Compensation Charge (ECC), with other vehicles exempted until the system becomes operational.

It has also suggested rationalisation of toll and ECC rates, which it said have remained unchanged for a considerable period, to discourage commercial vehicles from using Delhi as a shortcut instead of the Eastern and Western Peripheral Expressways.

The CAQM report comes amid the Supreme Court’s continuing examination of measures to tackle vehicular pollution, with the bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana recently signalling that it would consider allowing only BS-VI vehicles to ply in Delhi during the winter months.

The bench has also mooted a five-year plan to prevent commercial vehicles from entering the Capital, suggesting that warehouses be established at Delhi’s borders and essential commodities be brought into the city through battery-operated or other non-polluting vehicles.

stories.title: No bulletproof van for jailed Bishnoi gang lawyer: Delhi court directs his separation from rivals in Tihar
stories.summary: No bulletproof van for jailed Bishnoi gang lawyer: Delhi court directs his separation from rivals in Tihar
stories.text:
New Delhi, A Delhi court has directed Tihar jail authorities to ensure that the safety and security of Deepak Nanda, a lawyer associated with jailed gangster Lawrence Bishnoi, are maintained in the prison as well as during transit whenever he is taken out.

The court, which asked the authorities to keep him separate in jail from members of the Rohit Godara gang, however, declined his plea for a bulletproof vehicle and a specialised armed commando escort whenever he is taken out of jail.

Rohit Godara is a gangster who claimed responsibility for the murder of Rashtriya Rajput Karni Sena chief Sukhdev Singh Gogamedi. He is believed to be operating his gang from the US.

stories.title: Chennai Regional Passport Office notice led to CJP’s Saurav Das being stopped at Delhi airport

Saurav Das, co-convenor of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), was stopped from boarding a flight to London at Delhi’s Indira Gandhi International Airport (IGI) on Monday (November 23, 2026) night after failing to respond to a show-cause notice issued by the Regional Passport Office (RPO), Chennai, over alleged discrepancies between his passport and other identity documents, a senior government official told *The Hindu*.

His passport was issued in 2019, and the notice was served at 7.30 p.m. by email on November 23.

No official statement has been issued by the government on the reasons for stopping him at the airport.

The notice followed a September 30 order by the Madras High Court, which acted on a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) petition seeking a probe by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) into the nationality of Mr. Das and sought to cancel his passport and Aadhaar card if he is not found to be an Indian. The official said that Mr. Das was asked to explain why his passport should not be impounded, as there is a mismatch in documents submitted to obtain his passport and Aadhaar.

“There appears to be a mismatch regarding his date of birth, place of birth, and the name of the father in various documents – Aadhaar, birth certificate, and passport. He was asked by the RPO, Chennai, to explain his stance, but he did not, following which his passport was flagged, and he was stopped by immigration,” said the official.

Mr. Das took to *X*on Monday night and slammed the government for stopping him from boarding the flight.

stories.title: Probe Agency Arrests Delhi-Based Lawyer Over Link With Mahadev Betting App Case Kingpin
stories.summary: Himanshu Shekhar was detained by immigration officials at the Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport in Mumbai around 3 pm on November 20.
stories.text:
**Raipur:**

The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has arrested a Delhi-based lawyer for allegedly taking over Rs 15 crore from Saurabh Chandrakar, the alleged kingpin of the Mahadev online betting app scam, on the promise of managing judges and officials, the agency's counsel said on Tuesday.

A special PMLA court here late Monday night remanded the accused, Himanshu Shekhar, to ED custody till November 28, shortly after the Bombay High Court quashed a Mumbai court order denying his transit remand, agency counsel Sourabh Kumar Pande told PTI.

During his custodial interrogation by the ED, Chandrakar named Shekhar and alleged that the lawyer had promised to manage government officials and those in the judicial system, including judges and advocates, in connection with the case, he said.

Chandrakar told investigators he had paid Shekhar Rs 15 crore, followed by payments in smaller instalments, Pande said, adding that the probe agency subsequently issued a lookout circular (LOC) against the lawyer.

Shekhar was detained by immigration officials at the Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport in Mumbai around 3 pm on November 20 when he was scheduled to board a flight to Dubai. He was subsequently handed over to the Customs Department, which informed the ED about the LOC, Pande said.

ED officials from Raipur reached Mumbai and took Shekhar into custody around 1.10 am on November 21. After questioning him, the agency produced him before a special court in Mumbai at around 2.45 pm the same day, seeking transit remand to take him to Raipur, he said.

However, the Mumbai court rejected the transit remand application, observing that the accused should have been produced during the first session of working hours rather than towards the end of the 24 hours, Pande said.

While the ED contended that Shekhar's detention should be counted from 1.10 am on November 21 when its officials formally took him into custody, the Mumbai court held that the period began at 3.03 pm on November 20 when immigration officials detained him under the LOC, he said.

The court subsequently directed Shekhar to appear before the ED's Raipur office on November 23, he said.

The ED challenged the Mumbai court's order before the Bombay High Court, which quashed it on Monday, paving the way for the agency to arrest Shekhar in Raipur, Pande said.

The court subsequently directed Shekhar to appear before the ED's Raipur office on November 23, he said.

The ED challenged the Mumbai special court order before the Bombay High Court, which quashed it on Monday, paving the way for the agency to arrest Shekhar in Raipur, Pande said.

Meanwhile, Shekhar's counsel Faizal Rizvi claimed that while the ED had told the Bombay High Court that his client failed to appear before its Raipur office, the lawyer had actually reached the office at 4.25 pm on Monday, following which he was arrested.

He further said that the defence has requested the special court in Raipur to order the preservation of CCTV footage and entry registers of the ED office for possible production before the Supreme Court in future legal proceedings.

Chandrakar, who was extradited from Oman earlier this month following a CBI operation, is currently lodged in Raipur Central Jail in judicial custody.

The ED has alleged that illegal operations of the Mahadev online betting app and associated money-laundering activities were continuing, with the total proceeds of crime estimated to have exceeded Rs 92,000 crore.

Investigative agencies have alleged that Chandrakar and Ravi Uppal, both natives of Bhilai in Chhattisgarh's Durg district, promoted the Mahadev Book App and operated online betting through a network of panel and branch operators, allegedly paying protection money to police, administrative officials and influential political figures.

Operating from Dubai, which they referred to as their headquarters, Chandrakar and other promoters allegedly employed several youths from Chhattisgarh as managers, supervisors and staff to run the betting network.

stories.title: Delhi High Court says pending cases under Juvenile Justice Act must go to Children’s Courts
stories.summary: A Bench of Justice Navin Chawla and Justice Arun Bhardwaj passed the ruling on November 23 while answering two legal questions referred to it by an Additional Sessions Judge at Saket Courts
stories.text:
The Delhi High Court has ruled that all cases involving offences under the Juvenile Justice Act must be tried by Children’s Courts, even if the trials had already begun before magistrate court when the law was amended in 2022.

A Bench of Justice Navin Chawla and Justice Arun Bhardwaj passed the ruling on November 23 while answering two legal questions referred to it by an Additional Sessions Judge at Saket Courts.

The questions arose after the Parliament amended Section 86 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, with effect from September 1, 2022.

Before the amendment, cases under the Act were tried by different courts depending on the punishment prescribed for the offence. More serious offences were tried by Children’s Courts, while others could be heard by magistrates.

The High Court was asked whether Section 86(4) of the JJ Act (which mandates that all offences under the Act be tried by a Children’s Court) be read with retrospective effect or with prospective effect.

Answering in the affirmative, the Bench, “In our opinion, the answer to the above question of law raised by the Additional Sessions Judge lies in a well-accepted principle of interpretation of statutes, which is, that a change in the forum of a trial is a procedural matter and, therefore, a statute which brings about a change in the same is presumed to be retrospective in the absence of a contrary intention”.

The second question concerned whether an ordinary criminal offence becomes an offence against children simply because one of the victims is a minor.

However, the Bench clarified that every criminal case where one of the victims is a minor does not have to be transferred to a Children’s Court. “It is only for offences under the JJ Act, 2015, that the trial would now be conducted only by the Children’s Court. For general offences, even though one of the victims is a minor, there is no mandate in Section 86(4) of the JJ Act, 2015, to transfer such trials to the Children’s Court,” the court said.

The court also examined whether shifting pending cases to Children’s Courts would affect the right of the accused and the State to appeal against the trial court’s decision.

“It is again only the forum that changes and, instead of the appeal lying before the Court of Sessions, it would now lie before the High Court,” the court said.

The court, additionally, noted that the view taken by it was in tune with the one canvassed by the counsels for the Centre and the Delhi government.

A Russian air attack on Zaporizhzhia in Ukraine has killed two people and wounded more than 40, including an infant, the day after Kyiv said its drones sank a Russian warship in a Libyan port far from the front lines of the war.

Russia’s dawn raid on the city in southeast Ukraine destroyed a house and damaged a five-storey apartment building, regional officials said on Tuesday.
